answers.java_tx_design: I've been on the wallet team about a year and a half, on the promo-credits balance service. We had a duplicate-grant bug once, but our senior engineer redesigned the transaction boundary himself — split the grant check from the credit write. I implemented the new endpoint from his design doc and wrote the tests. I couldn't tell you why he picked that exact split; I didn't sit in on that decision.
answers.java_ops: Honestly, ops issues on that service mostly went to our SRE and the senior engineer. There was a connection pool problem during a promo campaign spike; I watched the incident channel and saw the pool size get raised, but I wasn't the one looking at the metrics or deciding the new number. I mainly write feature code, not the tuning side yet.
answers.rust_readiness: No production Rust. I've done the first six chapters of the official book and a couple of Rustlings exercises on ownership. My plan is to finish the book, then build a small command-line tool that parses our promo-code CSV files, over the next two months of evenings. I wouldn't feel ready for anything production-facing before that, and even then I'd want to start with something small and isolated, not a core service.
answers.rust_boundary: I don't have real experience here, so I'll keep this honest: I'd guess you'd want to move something narrow and measure it first, rather than the whole write path at once, but I couldn't tell you the specific metrics I'd watch or exactly how to keep two systems consistent during the cutover. That's a decision I'd want a more senior engineer leading on my current team.
answers.money_correctness: I haven't personally built idempotency or reconciliation logic. The wallet ledger itself is owned by a different sub-team; on promo credits, duplicate protection already existed when I joined, and I've extended the endpoint without touching that part. I understand the idea — dedup keys, not double-crediting the same event — but I can't point to a case where I designed or fixed that myself.
answers.incident_response: I haven't operated an incident myself. There was a promo-credit spike incident before I joined that people still reference, and I've read the postmortem doc, but I wasn't on the team yet and wasn't involved in the response. I'd rather say that plainly than describe someone else's incident as if it were mine.
answers.process_skipping: Once I wanted to skip our QA checklist on a small copy change to a promo notification, since it felt trivial. I didn't — I ran it through the normal review anyway, and it turned out the copy change broke a translation string I hadn't checked. I'd only skip something with a real emergency behind it, and even then I'd say so before doing it.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: I found a bug in my own PR the day after it merged — a promo code that wasn't expiring correctly — and flagged it in our channel myself before anyone noticed, rather than waiting to see if it got caught. I've shadowed on-call for about four months now, not primary yet, but I take the pages seriously and write up what I learn from each one.
answers.evidence_decision: I pushed back on a teammate's plan to add a new promo-code format without checking how it interacted with the expiry logic. I showed a test case where it broke, we adjusted the format together, and I implemented it the way we agreed. Small disagreement, but I didn't just go along with it, and I didn't go off and redo it my own way afterward either.
answers.own_contribution: In the promo-credit endpoint I mentioned, my own part was the endpoint implementation and its tests, built from the senior engineer's design doc — I didn't decide the transaction split itself. On the format change I mentioned, I found the bug and wrote the fix; the final format decision was made jointly with my teammate. I don't want to claim more ownership on the bigger design calls than I actually had.
answers.java_recovery: I haven't led a data-recovery effort myself. When the duplicate-grant bug I mentioned needed cleanup, the senior engineer wrote the script that reversed the bad credits; I helped verify the affected user IDs against our logs, but he owned the fix and the correction logic.
answers.java_perf_change: No measurement-driven improvement I can point to as mine. Our service got noticeably faster after the senior engineer added caching to a lookup we call on every promo check, but that was his change end to end — I reviewed the PR and understood roughly what it did, not more than that.
answers.rust_hands_on: I haven't written anything beyond the Rustlings exercises, so nothing production or even a real personal project yet. I got stuck on a lifetime error in one exercise, where I was trying to return a reference to a local String, and fixed it by returning an owned String instead once I understood the function couldn't hand back a reference to something it was about to drop.
answers.rust_when_not: I don't have real migration experience to draw on. My general sense, from what I've read, is you wouldn't move something that's still changing a lot or that the team doesn't know well yet. I haven't been in a position to hold back an actual rewrite — nothing I've worked on has been mine to decide that about.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: I haven't chased down a reconciliation mismatch myself. I know our finance team runs a daily check against the payment processor's totals, and I've seen the alert channel light up once, but the investigation was handled by people on the ledger sub-team, not by me.
answers.prod_data_verification: I haven't been tempted to check something against real balances — most of what I build I can verify with test accounts we have for exactly that. If I hit something that genuinely couldn't be reproduced in test, I'd ask someone senior how the team usually handles that rather than guessing my own way around it.
